The river prawn (Macrobrachium panamense) is a freshwater palaemonid decapod inhabiting rivers and estuaries along the Pacific coast of Central America. Newly hatched larvae are extremely small, with a wet weight at birth of approximately 0.000085 grams [Wwb = approximately 0.000085 grams], a value estimated from the egg dimensions of the related palaemonid Palaemon elegans. This minute larval mass reflects the species' planktonic larval strategy, in which newly released zoeae drift in estuarine waters before migrating upstream as post-larvae.

Growth proceeds through a series of larval and juvenile stages before the onset of sexual maturity. Individuals reach the total length at puberty of 5 centimeters [Lp = 5 centimeters], a value scaled from data on the smaller congener Palaemon elegans. At this size, the corresponding wet weight at puberty is approximately 10.54 grams [Wwp = approximately 10.54 grams], reflecting the substantial somatic investment achieved by the time reproductive maturity is reached.

Adults of Macrobrachium panamense ultimately attain a total length of 8 centimeters [Li = 8 centimeters], with a corresponding ultimate wet weight of approximately 43.2 grams [Wwi = approximately 43.2 grams]. This substantial adult body size, considerably larger than many marine palaemonids, is characteristic of freshwater Macrobrachium prawns, several of which are prized for their large size in artisanal and commercial fisheries throughout their range.

Reproductive output in this species is comparatively high for a decapod of its size. At a water temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C], the maximum reproductive rate reaches approximately 141 offspring per day [Ri = approximately 141 offspring per day], a value scaled from the relative fecundity documented for Palaemon elegans. Longevity in Macrobrachium panamense reaches a maximum of approximately 4.6 years [am = approximately 4.6 years] at the same reference temperature, a lifespan that, combined with high fecundity and substantial adult body size, supports the species' persistence in the seasonally variable rivers and estuaries of its native range at a temperature of 24 °C [T = 24 °C].
